To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

nitrate reductases from bacteria, fungi and plants have different quinol-binding sites, and that the electron transfer from quinols for nitrate reduction is a two-electron process that requires all of the FeS centers.

menadiol and menaquinol are the preferred physiological electron donors, that menadiol delivers its electrons at a different site on the enzyme than duroquinol, that the highest-potiential Fe-S centre is not required, but that the low-potential centre plays a key role in the reduction of nitrite and nitrate.

the steady-state kinetics and cross-inhibition experiments indicate that menaquinols and duroquinols deliver their electrons to nitrate reductases at different sites, and that the loss of the high-potential Fe/S centre of the beta subunit of nitrate reductates does not affect the activity of the enzyme with duroquinol as electron donor, but abolishes the activity with menaquinol.

the kinetics of nitrate reductases, which are membrane-bound enzymes involved in the reduction of nitro compounds in bacteria.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two quinol substrates of nitrate reductases have two different reaction sites on the enzyme, and that the two reaction pathways are different.
the two quinol pathways are different but not entirely separate.
menadiol and menaquinol are the natural substrates of the enzyme, but the mechanism of electron transfer from the quinols is still not clear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
menadiol and the other quinols of the respiratory chain are likely to be the physiological electron donors for nitrate reductases in Escherichia and Salmonella.
the reduction of nitrite by menadiol requires all of the FeS centres, whereas the reduction of nitroso-compounds by the quinol is not affected by the loss of an FeS centre of +80mV.
the Fe-S centres of nitrate reductases are not all involved in catalysis, but are required for optimal activity, with the highest-potentials Fe-S centre being important for the menadiol activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nitrate reductases are not simple enzymes, and that their kinetic properties are complex, reflecting the fact that they are involved in a complex physiological process.
the two quinol electron donors, duroquinol and dihydrophenazine (menadiol), have very different effects on the steady-state kinetics and on the activity of nitrate reductases.
nitrate reduction in vivo is probably catalyzed by the wild type enzyme and not the mutants with a missing Fe-S center.
